summary: A periodic index memo summarizing the RFCs numbered 2600 through 2699. It is a reference listing rather than a protocol specification, helping readers see what was published in that range.

eli5.summary: This is like a table of contents for a shelf of one hundred books, telling you what each one is about.

subtitle: A summary of one hundred RFCs published in a specific time period.

tldr.problem: Readers need a way to understand what happened in RFC publishing during a particular range of numbers.
tldr.mechanism: A human-readable index that lists each RFC from 2600 to 2699 with a brief one- or two-sentence summary of its purpose.
tldr.outcome: Serves as a quick reference for browsing RFCs in that range, but offers no analysis or connection between documents.

sections.title: An Index of RFCs 2600 Through 2699
sections.content:
This RFC is a status report: a lightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs numbered from 2600 to 2699. Each entry gives the RFC number, the author, the publication date, the title, and a one- or two-sentence summary of what the document is about.

Some RFCs in this range are on the Internet standards track (marked [STANDARDS-TRACK]), meaning they are moving toward or are at Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, or Full Standard status. Others are Informational or Experimental. The document notes that since standards status can change, the latest edition of "Internet Official Protocol Standards" (RFC 2600) should be consulted for the current state.
sections.eli5: This document lists one hundred RFCs, each with a short description so you can see what was published and pick out the ones you care about.

sections.title: What the Range Covers
sections.content:
The 100 RFCs from 2600 to 2699 span topics across the entire Internet protocol stack and infrastructure. Among them are standards for core protocols like HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616), LDAP control extensions (RFC 2696), PPP over SONET (RFC 2615), and Layer Two Tunneling (RFC 2661).

There are also RFCs on security and cryptography: S/MIME extensions (RFC 2634), Diffie-Hellman key agreement (RFC 2631), RADIUS MIBs (RFCs 2618-2621), and HTTP digest authentication (RFC 2617). Informational documents in the range include benchmarking guidance (RFC 2644), performance analysis (RFC 2682), and periodic reviews like this one itself (RFC 2699).

The range includes many MIB definitions for network management, protocol-specific design considerations (like NFS Version 4, RFC 2624), and documentation of vendor protocols (like Cabletron and Nortel implementations).
sections.eli5: The range includes big important protocols like HTTP and security methods, plus a lot of smaller documents that help manage networks and explain how systems work together.

sections.title: Standards Track vs. Other Categories
sections.content:
RFCs in this range are divided into several categories. Many are marked [STANDARDS-TRACK], meaning they are proposals for Internet standards. The path to standardization is described in RFC 2026 and typically moves through three stages: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, and Full Internet Standard.

Others are Informational, meaning they convey information to the Internet community without proposing a standard. These cover topics like FYI documents (RFC 2664, "Questions and Answers for New Internet Users"), vendor protocol specifications (RFC 2643, Cabletron SecureFast VLAN), and reports like this one.

The range also includes Experimental RFCs, which describe protocols or techniques that are not yet ready for standardization. Examples include S-HTTP security extensions (RFC 2659) and SPKI certificate work (RFCs 2692-2693).
sections.eli5: Some RFCs are on the path to becoming real standards; others are just sharing information or experiments that people are trying out.

sections.title: How to Use This Document
sections.content:
To find a specific RFC in the 2600-2699 range, scan the summary table for the title that matches your interest. If you want to understand the state of a particular area in 1999-2000 (when these RFCs were published), the grouped descriptions show what work was happening in areas like security, networking, management, and messaging.

Note that the summaries are very brief. To understand what an RFC actually says, you must read the RFC itself. This document is a guide to help you navigate the range and decide which documents to examine in detail.
sections.eli5: Use the list to find the RFC you need, then read that RFC itself to learn what it really says.
